blocks.x: All right, we're going to... Okay, we're back. This is the interview with Tommy Ridgely, April 23rd, 1986. This is a continuation, and this is real number one for that date. My name's Tad Jones, and we're at Tommy Ridgely's house at 2... 14... 14... On Avenue, right. In River Ridge, Louisiana. I wasn't sure where to start this time. One thing we sort of hit on at the end was...

We're on reel number two with Tommy Richley, April 23rd, 1986. Okay, I think we're gonna get back to your discography, because I've got a list here, you know, of records. And I think most of it, it's got the names of the players and et cetera. But there are a couple of tunes that I just want to ask you a couple of questions about. Maybe more than a couple here. Your earliest sessions for Imperial, there's one song in particular, it was called Shrewsbury.
Shrewsbury, that's my first record.
That you wrote Shrewsbury Blues?

Yeah, I wrote Shrewsbury Blues and I wrote the flip side, I think it was Early Dawn Boogie. And I tell you what, back then I was influenced by Roy Brown, T-Bone Walker, and mostly Roy Brown, because Roy Brown was very, very popular at that time. And I remember, see this is the beginning, this is right in the early stages of my singing career. I was singing on Shrewsbury Road by Sam Gennaro's place, and Bama had a Dixieland band there. And I used to go in there and sing, you know, and we would get a quarter, somebody would give us a quarter
and stuff for singing a specific song.

And I used to do Long About Midnight, but it was because I could sing ballads that really kind of take the musicians off. You know, I liked the idea, you know, I'd come in and sing, but I could sing ballads. Right. And so this was, you know, that was the very beginning. But Shrewsbury Blues, when I left Bama, and I went with Earl Anderson up in Gertown by the, what was it called?
Starlight.

Starlight. Yeah, okay. And I was singing, but that's when Dave Bitholomew, and I guess they heard about me, because Dave Bitholomew, Al Young, who had the record shop, one-stop record shop on Rampart Street, they came to listen to me. And I guess they liked what I heard, what they heard, because that Monday I had an appointment, and I met Dave Bitholomew, and at One Stop Record Shop with me, Al Young, and we went to Charles Levy's office, wherever that was, or somewhere. And, well, they signed me up. And I signed everything they put before me. And then I recorded Shrewsbury Blues, Early Dawn Boogie, and I guess I did Four Sides.
Well, yeah, I see. Yeah.
But I know, I know early enough Shrewsbury Blues was the first release.
And that was about Shrewsbury Blues?
Yeah, that was right down the causeway. It was Shrewsbury's location from...
Yeah, give me the bio.

Yeah, it's from, I say, from the river to the track, the first track. Because across the track... Which track? Well, it's Public Belt Railroad. Okay. See, that's right, that's right. That's that section, that's Shrewsbury. Now, and it's, I guess it's from La Bar Road all the way to Severn Avenue. Okay. Over, you know, in Whip. That's Shrewsbury.
Well, you're kind of right on the edge almost.
Yeah, I live, I live right on the, I was living on the causeway. Yeah. See, we used to call it Harlem Avenue.
Which was Harlem Avenue.
Yeah, right. And, because that's where, that's where I grew up. Well, okay, I recorded Shrewsbury Blues and it was a big hit in Shrewsbury.
Yeah. Was it a big hit in New Orleans?

Yeah, well, it was a big hit in New Orleans. In fact, I have requests for it now. I don't remember that song. But it's in this album. Uh-huh, yeah. And, you know, I listened to, I listened to the record and, and it sound better now than it did then because I think they were able to take some hiss out and you get a little bit better quality of what you can hear now than a long time ago. But I used to hate that, you know, after, later on I listened to that bad sound. See, because in recording, Cosmo would look up and get a good sound. Good sound didn't come every day. You record me, maybe two, three, four, five different people come in and record. He didn't get no good sound and then he'd look up on one. But Shrewsbury Blues was my first release on Imperium.
Okay, there was another song called Lavinia. Lavinia.
Lavinia.
Was that about a certain person? Lavinia.

No, that just was a song. I'll tell you, well, there was a story I recorded. That song, that's the only song that I feel like I stole from somebody in all my career as a musician. Well, I got that song from Blazer Boy. What Blazer Boy's name was? George Stevenson, was that? George Stevenson, I think so. Well, anyway, he used to be at the, at the, not the Tijuana. I went to the hotel around there on, but I was around about three. But anyway, in this place, I went in there one night where Hugh Smith, guitar, Slim, and all of us, we used to go in there every night. And the band had a band there every night. I went in there one night and Blazer Boy was singing this thing. Oh, LaBerta, oh, LaBerta, don't you hear me calling you. And boy, that stuck with me, stuck with me. And so I went home and I wrote Lavinia. And I recall that was a pretty big hit around New Orleans. The one? Yeah, the one. See, back then playing with Dave Otholomew, we played for, almost identical to the way I play today. He played for all the social clubs, he got a lot of black social clubs, played for all of the high school. See, Dave, we were pretty popular at that. And them school kids love it at Lavinia.
Okay, I had a song called Junie Mae. Junie Mae, Junie Mae.

That was just another song, don't you hear me. See, that was one of those, you know what, I haven't heard Junie Mae in yet. I like to hear that. But anyway, I remember because Junie Mae was one of these eight ball kind of things, like a progression like Lord of Miss Claudia. Oh, okay. Da-dee-da-dee, da-dee-dee, ba-da-dee-dee. I like to hear Junie Mae.
I was wondering, I thought it was on that album. It's on that album.
I don't think, no. Junie Mae's not on this album. No, it's not on that album.
I know, I haven't heard it in a long time, I think I've got it on tape somewhere.
I'm going to try to find it.
Okay, and there's a title here that really interests me, and it's Monkey Man.
Well, I ain't going to be a monkey man no more.
Now that was a- I wanted to know what that meant.

Well, that just was a, Monkey Man, what it mean is that I, in essence, I ain't going to be your fool no more. Oh. That's all. And, see, this was a, like back then, Joe Turner, you know, that's called a, you walk on a bandstand and they play the shuffle and B flat, and I could sing Monkey Man. Right. Yeah, you know, or either any one of Joe Turner songs, you know, back then, because that's just a shuffle. Yeah. And, see, Joe Turner would say shuffle in G, and he would get to singing in the key of G. And Joe Turner never would tell you a key of his song. He would get to talking in that key. And he had this natural pitch to every, all of his songs, and just before then, and we can find on the piano, we know what it was. And when you go into the song, . So you backed Joe Turner?
Oh, many, many, many, many, many, many times.

Yeah. See, at the Dew Drop, that's another thing. See, I played at the Dew Drop at one stretch, and I'll say I've been trying to remember, it had to be before I went to Milano, and I think around 1954. I played there almost two years straight. And I think so, because when I left the Dew Drop, I went to, I went up on Oak Street. So it was either 55, all of, I think all of 55 I was in the Dew Drop. And part of 56, you know, maybe the end of 54, all of 55, part of 56, I was playing Dew Drop every night. Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Making about $15.
About a night? Uh-huh. Was that kind of standard?
Kind of, yeah, kind of standard. $15, well, $10 was the standard thing. See, at one time it was eight. I think it went up to ten, and I think I probably made fifteen.
Now, was that union scale, or was that what Dwight paid? No, that was union scale.
Eight dollars was union scale. And what, what assignment did you get it? Well, no, no, well, I made, well, if I made fifteen, the assignment must have got eight. Oh, okay. Or maybe ten.
As leader.
Yeah. Can I tell you this? I remember the first time I made a hundred dollars. In one night? Yeah.
You're talking one night? Yeah.

First time. We were, and this was in 1953. 52? Or 53. And I was with Big Curtis. He came, got me, we're going on the road. He went to Nashville. But Christmas night, we played in Opelousa. Packed up like this. I don't know what it was. I can't remember, but I do know this. When we knocked off that night, because we, from there was going on to Nashville. Curtis gave me a lot of relief. And I was with Big Curtis. We were, he came, got me, we're going on the road. We headed to Nashville. But Christmas night, we played in Opelousa. And they had a club called White Eagle. Everybody at my age, you know, they all heard nobody White Eagle. Packed up like this.
I don't know what it was.
I can't remember, but I do know this. When we knocked off that night, because we, from there was going on to Nashville. Curtis gave me ten, ten dollar bills. I couldn't, all this for me?
Yeah.

But the sad part was that he gave the band fifteen dollars. And they all came to me. Man, look who Curtis gave up. He said, man, all the people he had out there, man, all that ball. And so, I was, but I wasn't in charge of no band, you know. But they came to me to tell me. And so I went to Curtis. I said, man, I said, look Curtis, okay, you treated me nice. I said, man, you don't give the fellas fifteen dollars on a Christmas night. Yeah. So he gave them five more. And we only had five pieces. Just another one of them little things, you know. All right.
You left Imperial. Was there any reason why you left Imperial? No. Did they give you a reason?
No, the records slowed down. You know, I think I had about five or six releases on Imperial, maybe more than that.
Okay.

And evidently, you know, I did fairly well because the record company dropped you like a hot potato when you don't sell. But I had a few releases with Imperial. And with a slowdown, I left them and I went to, I think the next company. Yeah, I think it was Dekka.
Dekka, okay.
Talking about Dekka.
Yeah. And your big song with Dekka was Tra La La.

Okay, yeah, well that's something to talk about. Was Tra La La story? Okay, I wrote Tra La La. I never forget how I wrote it. I wrote Tra La La. See, because it was that Lord of Miss Claude kind of progression again. Laying across my bed, I'm living on Andover Street. That's how I wrote the song. And I had a little piano out on a porch that used to cut down bang on. Well then I wrote that song there and I had this song and I told it to everybody. So we finally got around to recording. Never did have a flip side for Tra La La. I never had one. I didn't have nothing. And so there was this song Ray Tyler had wrote called T-Gym. And so what they did, they made a deal with Dekka Records. Cosmo did I guess. And so they put Tra La La on one side and they had T-Gym on the flip side. T-Gym was a tune that Tyler had wrote and Dave Atholomew had put this on the flip side of a commercial thing he made for Jackson Buret. Drank Jags Buret. Yeah. Drank Jags Buret. Okay T-Gym, the original T-Gym was on the flip side of that. So they put T-Gym on the flip side of my record.
Now my record came out doing fantastic.

Louisiana, all in the south, in the southern market. Now Dave Atholomew had already told me, said, man, well look up, we gonna do like, and it's his words, we gonna do like Arthur Prysock and Buddy Johnson with Arthur Prysock. You see, in the record back then, Arthur Prysock's name was up in the right hand corner as a singer, Buddy Johnson was out here. So this is what Dave said, it was gonna do with me. So when the record came out, the people didn't look at who was singing, they look at Dave Atholomew. Okay, Dave had a record, had a contract with the company he was recording for. We did Country Boy, yeah.
He was still with Imperial.

No, no, he didn't have a contract, a recording contract with him. The recording contract was with this company that, Deluxe. Deluxe. Deluxe. Deluxe. Deluxe said, if Dave don't get his name off the record, they was gonna sue. So, okay. So what I had to do, they said I had to come to New York. Cosmo and I, they were the first, they were not heard of too much. Cosmo and I was the first black, white to get a sleeping bird train from here in New Orleans. And this is true. We talk about this now, me and Cosmo. Nobody said nothing about it. I had the opera, Cosmo had the lower, and we went to New York. And so it had to be 1952. And I went to New York, but I didn't know that they had already sold me out. See, but I went to New York in order for them to get the correct lyrics, and they wanted to know exactly how the song go for the Griffin Brothers. And when I get up there, a Lucky Milner, band leader, he invited me over to his office after he heard me in the studio. I suppose I recorded. But anyway, he said, man, look, I want you to write lyrics down for me. And Lucky Milner, light-skinned man with straight hair. And I remember, because I just got his name straight. I forgot him. It was Lucky Milner. But anyway, I wrote the lyrics down for Lucky Milner, and I think the next day I went in the studio and I recorded. I recorded with some musicians that didn't know no more about them eight-bar blues and the man in the mood. I had to get on the piano and show them how it thing go. True.
I think one of these black or white musicians?

Black musicians. Well, in New York, they don't know about what's going on down here. And so we recorded a jungle-up version of Tra-La-La. And I stayed in New York. The only time I saw Cosmo was when I was in the studio, because I stayed at a hotel downtown New York. I forgot the name of the hotel, but it was downtown. Cosmo had relatives in New York, so he stayed by the hotel. And the only time I saw Cosmo was when I recorded and after that I didn't see him. But the deal was made then that with Cosmo, Dave Othlame wasn't there, but he was part of it, with the Griffin Brothers. They recorded the tune, and by the time I got back to New Orleans, my tune had been recorded by the Griffin Brothers and was all over. And they got his old record.
So I was sold out. So the reason for you to go to New York wasn't for you to record the song.
They wanted to find out exactly what was happening with it. And you know what?
I have an album over there with the Griffin Brothers, and I just got it.

But anyway, and I look at it, and I remember how this thing went down. Now, what happened later on, I said about four or five years after that, they had this white belt. He was a sailman at Patterson Pontiac on Galveston Canal. I went in there. And my cousin was buying a car, a 1956 Pontiac. And so I was a cosigner with him. We were talking.
And the guy said, man, I know you.

And then I told him, he said, oh, yeah. And then he said, let me tell you something. He said, did you ever get any money out of this Tra-La-La deal? I said, hey, what kind of money? He said, oh, some money was paid off. He said, I know it. He said, Cosmo got some money, Dave Bithalemus got some money. He said, and I was out on the road selling your record. He said, and it was selling. He said, but all of a sudden, I had to drop your record. He said, I came back in raising hell, and they gave me some money to shut me up. I'm telling you, just like that. He said, and I'll tell you what. He said, I ain't in the record business no more. And he said, if you want to go to Colt and try to get some money, he said, I'll be your witness. And I said, I don't forget about it. Dave Bithalemus, Cosmo. So is. And I don't know how much it made, but I know a deal was made, because the Griffin Brothers, yeah, they are.
Yeah.
And I read about it. It's on the back of that album right over there now. And I said, oh, well, that's another one of my misfortunes in this business.
I ain't in it yet. I'm looking at this. It's got some other songs.
What was it?
On the deck of Anything But Love.
Yeah, I remember Anything But Love. You know, I have.
Once in a lifetime.
Once in a lifetime. See, I wrote all of those things.
So you must have done four tracks.
I did, yeah. I did four tunes. Yeah, I did four tunes. Yeah, I did four tunes. But the Trial Laugh version never came out. They never released that.
Well, they did originally, but it was pulled.
Yeah, mine was pulled.
No, see, yeah.
The recording was Dave and New Orleans. But the one that I recorded in New York. See, the one that was supposed to have to get Dave off.
That was just a demo. Right. Right, right.
And I always think about that.
Well, then, from there, obviously, you parted company with Decker.
Yeah, I parted company with Decker. I don't think so.
And then you went with Atlantic.

Right, okay. I had a, the success with Atlantic was, I had, I'm going to cross that river. Okay, that was a slow tune that was very, very successful for me. And even right now, I can go on the other side of the river and go up the river, go on to Edgar, Vashera, you know, round up that way. All I got to do is sing. I'm going to cross that river. See, I used to put two songs together. I'm going to cross that river and the things I used to do. That's all I had to do. Kill audience. Kill? Yes, indeed. And right now, if I go to see, if I go to Edgar, all I got, oh, the Creole, oh, Tommy Ridge there. The things that, the things, the things that I used to do, and I'm going to cross that river. And very, very successful. And then after that, I had Jam Up. Now, I talked to, I talked to Jerry Wexler. But what was between that?
Well, I want to get back to going to cross that river because you had some, who are you musicians on going to cross that river?
Oh, I want to cross, oh, well, that was the Dave Otholomew's band.
Okay.

That was the Dave Otholomew's band. And Miss Gladys DeVore, the lady, I wonder if she's still living. I know the lady got to be, I saw her about three years ago. She live up on Valens near Chappatulas. Yeah, near Chappatulas, a magazine, near Magazine. Yeah. And she wrote, I'm going to cross that river. But it was the regular Dave Otholomew band. The regular, you know.
Who was your piano player?
I think it was Salvador Ducet. Now, that's pulling my memory.
I thought it was Ray Charles. That's what it was.
Oh, yeah.
That's what I was saying.

I thought you had a pretty good piano player. Okay. Okay. Okay, yeah. Now you see that ring the bell. Okay. Now, now, now, I can remember. Okay. Ray Charles was in town. Ray Charles was in town because he stayed around New Orleans quite a bit because he wasn't the superstar like he is now. And he would live at Foster's down the street from the Dew Drop, but he was hanging in the Dew Drop. And Atlantic came in town and Ray Charles was having these records with Atlantic. And when they came in to record me, well, Ray Charles did. He was, he's the producer. He produced the record. And I remember Jerry Wexler told Ray Charles to play, but don't play like Ray Charles. Don't sound like Ray Charles. And he tried to do it. But if you would listen to the flip side of I'm Gonna Cross That River, which was I'm Loop.
I think that was the song we haven't told you.
No, no, not Loop. No, Lord and My Baby. Lord and My Baby. Okay, that was a tune that you could hear Ray Charles. Ray Charles finally got into being Ray Charles. But I'm Loop was on him, period.
Yeah, and we didn't talk about that.
We sure didn't talk about that. Okay, let's talk about that. Now, now, come back.
Okay, okay.
That was a tune, yeah. It was a tune that was sent down here for me to record by Lou Chud, I think. And we did a cover on somebody from Chicago. Who it was, I don't know.
I'll have to find out.

Okay, well, it was from Chicago. Anyway, they sent us, when we were in the studio waiting for the song, the band was sitting there waiting, the song came by playing. And when it got the song, it rushed on to the studio. I had never heard it. And so the lady took it and she typed the word. And then they gave the song to me. And I went in the booth. And I learned the song. And then I went in the studio and recorded it. And that was, well, what we did, we did an exact copy of that record, whoever that was. And that was pretty good. It was well, well. See, I always think about Ernest MacLaine, the guitar player, and the solo he had on I'm Blue. You see, I don't know if you noticed, but that song is not in this album either. See, that's on him period. But you see, all of that is in period. But I'm Luke, it's not in there.
But I'm sure it's on that album.
Uh-uh. Ooh.
Wait.
It is. No, they didn't put, that was one, they didn't put, I put this back up. Let's see. That way. You know, I'm going to have to listen again. Junie Mae.
Junie Mae is on. Yeah. Uh-huh. Monk and Mae. And Luke is on that record. Yeah.

Oh. Oh. Okay. Hmm. And you see, I put this up there. Now, I'm going to tell you something about this record. You know, almost Slim was the one who called me about this record. And he said that somebody planned on putting it out. Okay, fine by me. But if they had given me a few records, I would have been happier.
So they haven't sent you this?
This is it.
That's it? That's it. Okay.
One record. And, um.
Are they sending you royalties at all on this one?
Uh.
Are they saying they're going to send you royalties or anything?
Well, he said they said they were going to do something. I'm, you know, I know they know where I am. Because Slim talked to me. I'll tell you what. I do know this. I found out Slim.
He gets mechanical.
This is his project. Yeah. See, all of the New Orleans things. You go to, you go to Metronome. You're going to see a wreck.
Yeah.
All of the things that Slim's project.
Mm-hmm.
Now, how it's worked, I don't know. But it's Slim. And you know what? My good friend, Mr. David Alamute.
Mm-hmm.
I haven't talked to him yet. He won't call me about this. Won't tell me nothing about it.
Mm-hmm. Awesome. So, just for the record, you said this is on the, it's a French label. Right. Patier Marconi. And this is a series that's been coming out all year on New Orleans.

Right. On all New Orleans people. And I do know that because the guy told me, he said, if I want to find anything out about this, I have to get in touch with Alamute Slim. He called him by name. Slim's real. Slim's real. Yeah.
Jeff Honish. Honish.
Okay. Yeah. All right.
Have you talked to him?
He didn't tell me nothing. He gave me to give me some old address. He's talking about I can write to somebody in France. Let you do that for me. That's right. Yeah.

Let's get back to Atlantic. Okay. And there's something that you're coming from Imperial. Okay. Well, after, after. Between what I'm saying, what's the difference between, say, Alucha and Jerry Wexler?
A hundred percent. It's just like going from north, turning around and going south.
Really?

Yeah. First of all, Jerry Wexler was the type of man at that time. And from what I can gather, he hasn't changed. I used to call Jerry Wexler. I'd get on my phone and call Jerry Wexler. Me and him talk just like we talk. I could never do that with Luchette. In fact, I think I remember seeing Luchette once. But Wexler was, that's why they were so successful, I think. He was ideal. Everybody liked him. He found out they had talent in New Orleans and every week. Jerry Wexler and Armand Erdogan, he was down here. And everybody got to like him. And that's how myself, Professor Longhair, quite a few other people. But I know me and Fest, we were coming. And we wound up with pretty good records. See, because Jam Up, Jam Up have been in, in fact, from Rockland Standard, was recently released again. But it had been in about, I think, six different albums. And I had gold. I don't have a gold record, but I know it. So he just didn't make it a gold. But it had been all over the world. It had been theme songs for so many different rock shows. And this is all over the world. So that was successful. And you know what? I was talking to Jerry. Like I said, when Fest died, Jerry Wexler and I were talking. And he said, you know what I'm talking about? He said, I always think about that tune. See, first it was Thomas Hop. That's the first name. He said, you know, we contemplated with that name. He said, so we changed it. I didn't have anything to do with changing the name. They changed it. Jam Up. And then it was Jam Up, Twist. And then it came out in the all blues, some kind of album. You know, and see, that's one of the few records that I made that I got a few dollars off. Quite a bit.
Yeah, something I wanted to say. You told me, we talked about this last time, you actually got statements from Atlanta.

Oh, all kind of statements. And I have, right now I have checks. One penny. I think I have about three or four of them right down there right now. See, Atlantic, see that's why I say when you deal with big companies, you really don't have to worry about them not paying you. Because they're too big to mess around with a few dollars for you. Big people, I mean, it's the small people that want to mess around with the dollars for you. And I ain't got a penny. And I got quite a few pennies from Atlanta. You know, but I appreciate this and I know that if there's any money for me that Atlantic has, I don't worry about it. They're going to find some kind of way to get it to me. And I can't say that for Imperial because I've never received nothing from Imperial. I mean, when I say nothing, literally nothing. But I believe my money went in the other direction. I just didn't get it. Do I have to call a name?
Do I have to call his name? Okay. All right.

That's where the money went. Now, you know what? We can talk about all the records I made. But there's one other record. Okay. Okay. We talk about, let's talk about this particular tune here first. Which one? The one that Fats Domino recorded.
Which is? I Live My Life. Live My Life. Okay. Okay. Which one?
I'm a co-writer with Dave Bartholomew.
Right. On that tune.

Okay. Fats Dominow recorded it. Dave Bartholomew told me, and I tell this to the world because it's just exactly how he told me. He said, either, first he said, he believed that when Fats recorded that song, him and Fats, they had part ways. They were mad with each other. So he didn't make that record with Fats. Then he told me, this is another time, he said, you know, Fats recorded it, but he wanted to take your name off. That's the way he wanted it. Now, this, I'm, you know, there's some things you have to remember. These are the two things, statements that I got direct from Dave Bartholomew. And I have never received a call. Well, I found out.
And I had to think. You'd be credited on this album.
Yeah, I know. But.
The Pathé McConey album.

I had to be credited because it's right. You see, in the Czech BMI, I am the co-writer. It's BMI. But just did. And so they try to say, well, the spelling of the title, I live my life, which is mine. And in Fats Domino, I lived L-I-V-E-B, my life.
Okay, that's good.
Yeah. That's one of the other excuses. But, okay, the book lists that as a million dollars, Fats Domino. Okay, where's my money?
Yeah.
Okay, now, there's another record that I wrote and recorded with Rick Records.
Mm-hmm.
Double I Whammy.
Double I Whammy, okay. Okay.
Freddie King came down here, and he was on the cause. He was living on the causeway at Marino's Motel, and he and I got to be buddy buddies for a while. He was here because his cause broke down.
Right.
And I gave him one of my records that just came out on Rick. Freddie King went back to Dallas, and he recorded a tune called San Jose. And if you listen to San Jose and listen to Double I Whammy.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Thank you.
Reel number three, April the 23rd, 1986 with Tommy Richland. So we're talking about William and Freddie King.

This was a tune I recorded with Rick Records, and it was a good thing. It was one of the few tunes that I did with my band, my arrangement, my song, you know, the whole thing. But anyway, this was my band. It was the original, one of the Untouchables things that we did. And it had a good sound. And while Freddie King was in town, his car had broke down. He was living on the causeway at Marino's Motel. I'm a saxophone player in my band.
And he owned the hotel hotel?
